demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Mariam Haddad was 31 when she sought treatment, a divorced social media manager who had built a career around staying composed, responsive, and quick. The event that fractured that sense of herself happened on an ordinary late afternoon drive home from work. She had been inching through traffic after a long day, distracted for a split second as her phone lit up on the passenger seat with work notifications she did not answer. When the line of cars ahead slowed, she braked too late and struck a cyclist crossing in front of her lane. She still remembers the sickening thud and the way time seemed to collapse around the sight of his body hitting the pavement. What has stayed with her most sharply is the smell: hot rubber, engine heat, and a metallic, burnt odor that she says comes back “like it’s in the room.” In the immediate aftermath she was coherent enough to call 911, but later she found she could not describe the sequence without stopping mid-sentence, knowing exactly what had happened and yet unable to find words for it.

In the weeks that followed, Mariam became preoccupied with what the accident said about her. She had come to believe that a decent, careful person would not have done what she did, even by accident, and this conviction spread into a broader mistrust of herself. She second-guessed small decisions at work, reread posts before scheduling them, and hovered over routine approvals as if one careless click could hurt someone again. She often thought that the person she had become was unrecognizable to her and that something in her had been permanently damaged. Those beliefs seemed to shape the way the memory returned: sometimes she would think about the crash and be flooded by the smell of hot rubber and metal, and other times she would describe it flatly, almost with surprise at her own numbness, as if the scene had happened to a stranger. Even that emotional deadness frightened her, because to Mariam it seemed like proof that she was no longer the person she had been.

Her work environment kept confronting her with moments she could not fully predict. In the open-plan office, coworkers often tapped her shoulder to ask about a campaign revision or a client comment, and she would jolt violently, heart racing, turning with alarm before she knew where she was. A sudden touch on the subway, a pedestrian stepping too close in the crosswalk outside her building, even the abrupt movement of a cyclist passing her window could make her react as though danger were already present. These false alarms were not random to her. She was certain she could no longer trust herself to judge what was safe or what was happening around her, and that sense of being fundamentally unreliable kept her on edge. The more she saw herself as someone who had already caused catastrophic harm once, the more her body behaved as if another disaster were always about to break open.

When the memory intruded, it intensified that state immediately. Catching a whiff of overheated brakes in a parking garage or exhaust in city traffic could bring back the smell from the accident so vividly that she felt transported to the roadside. At other times the recollection came stripped of feeling, just visual fragments and facts, and that peculiar numbness did not calm her; it made her more alarmed. She would think, if I can remember this without feeling anything, what else is wrong with me? In those moments her fear, guilt, and shame surged together, and she became jumpier for hours afterward, reacting to ordinary noises and unexpected touch as if they signaled fresh threat.

That pattern also ran in the other direction. After a day spent braced against startle and scanning her surroundings, the accident felt closer and easier to trigger. By evening, if she had been bumped on the train twice or startled in the office, she was more likely to smell the crash again in her mind when she closed her apartment door, or to sit on her couch unable to put any of it into words. Her own constant alarm seemed to pull the memory nearer. And once she had been set off repeatedly, she judged herself even more harshly: a normal person would have moved on, she thought; a trustworthy person would not react like this. Each flare of fear and each reflexive jolt to unexpected touch became, for Mariam, further evidence that she was altered for the worse.

Over months, her world narrowed. She arranged to work from home more often, partly to avoid the shoulder taps and crowded commute that kept setting her off. She delayed decisions until colleagues followed up twice, and one supervisor commented that she seemed hesitant in a role that used to suit her confidence. Mariam heard this as confirmation that she was no longer herself. By the time she came to treatment, what finally pushed her to ask for help was not only the persistence of the memories, but the fear that her whole life was reorganizing around them. She was frightened that she had become someone permanently dangerous, permanently diminished, and she wanted desperately to know whether she could ever trust herself again.
